differential: Adrenal Tumor
An androgen-secreting adrenal tumor can cause rapid-onset hirsutism and virilization in a prepubertal child.
Non-classic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
This genetic disorder can present in early childhood with signs of androgen excess, including accelerated hair growth.
Exogenous Androgen Exposure
Accidental contact with topical androgen preparations used by an adult can lead to rapid virilization in a child.
Ovarian Tumor
A rare but serious cause of hyperandrogenism, an androgen-producing ovarian tumor would explain the rapid onset of symptoms.
Idiopathic Premature Pubarche
This is a benign condition characterized by the early appearance of pubic hair without other signs of puberty or underlying pathology.
eliminated: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
This is a diagnosis of adolescence and adulthood and is not applicable to a 5-year-old prepubertal child.
Congenital Hypertrichosis
The patient's hair growth has a recent onset of 2 months, which rules out a condition that would be present from birth.

differential: Central Precocious Puberty
This is the most common cause of precocious puberty in girls, resulting from premature activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
The non-classic form can present with premature pubarche and axillarche due to excess adrenal androgen production.
Adrenal Tumor
A virilizing adrenal neoplasm can secrete high levels of androgens, causing rapid progression of pubic and axillary hair growth.
Ovarian Tumor
A hormone-secreting ovarian tumor (e.g., granulosa cell tumor) is an important cause of gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty.
Exogenous Hormone Exposure
Accidental exposure to topical androgens or estrogens can cause a rapid onset of secondary sexual characteristics.
eliminated: Premature Adrenarche
This diagnosis is inconsistent with the advanced Tanner stage 4 development, which indicates a more profound and systemic pubertal process.

differential: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor
This is the most common estrogen-producing ovarian malignancy in children, fitting the presentation of isosexual precocious puberty and an ovarian mass.
Functional ovarian cyst
A large, autonomous follicular cyst can secrete high levels of estrogen, causing peripheral precocious puberty and appearing as a mass on ultrasound.
McCune-Albright syndrome
This syndrome can present with gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty due to recurrent, estrogen-producing ovarian cysts, which would appear as a mass.
Ovarian thecoma
This benign stromal tumor can produce estrogen, leading to isosexual precocious puberty, although it is less common than granulosa cell tumors in childhood.
Ovarian gonadoblastoma
This rare tumor can be hormonally active and is a consideration for an ovarian mass causing precocious puberty, particularly in patients with underlying gonadal dysgenesis.
eliminated: Central precocious puberty
The presence of an autonomous estrogen-producing ovarian mass indicates a peripheral, gonadotropin-independent cause rather than premature HPG axis activation.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
This condition typically causes virilization from excess androgens, not isosexual precocious puberty with high estrogen and an ovarian mass.

differential: Granulosa cell tumor
This diagnosis is confirmed by histopathology showing Call-Exner bodies, which explains the estrogen-secreting ovarian mass and resulting isosexual precocious puberty.
Ovarian thecoma
This benign stromal tumor can also secrete estrogen, presenting as an ovarian mass causing precocious puberty.
Ovarian germ cell tumor
Certain germ cell tumors can be hormonally active, presenting as an ovarian mass and causing precocious puberty.
McCune-Albright syndrome
This syndrome can cause peripheral precocious puberty via autonomous ovarian estrogen production, though it typically involves cysts rather than a solid mass.
Juvenile Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor
Although often androgenic, these tumors can sometimes produce estrogen and present as an ovarian mass with signs of precocity.
eliminated: Central precocious puberty
The presence of an estrogen-secreting ovarian mass indicates a peripheral, not central, cause of puberty.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
This condition causes androgen excess, which is inconsistent with the patient's signs of estrogen-driven (isosexual) precocious puberty.
Exogenous estrogen exposure
The identification of an endogenous ovarian tumor as the source of estrogen rules out an external exposure.

differential: Non-classic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
This genetic disorder is a common cause of androgen excess that can present in childhood with premature hair growth.
Androgen-secreting Adrenal Tumor
The rapid 2-month onset of hair growth in a young child is highly concerning for a neoplasm producing excess androgens.
Premature Adrenarche
This is a relatively common and benign condition involving early maturation of the adrenal glands, leading to pubic and/or axillary hair growth.
Exogenous Androgen Exposure
Accidental exposure to topical androgen products used by a household member can cause rapid virilization in a young child.
Androgen-secreting Ovarian Tumor
Although less common than adrenal sources, an ovarian neoplasm is an important consideration for androgen excess in a prepubertal girl.
eliminated: Classic Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
This condition typically presents at birth with ambiguous genitalia or in infancy with a salt-wasting crisis.
Congenital Hypertrichosis
This would be present from birth, not have an acute onset over the past two months.

differential: Premature adrenarche
This is the most common cause, representing a benign, early maturation of adrenal androgen production without other signs of puberty.
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
This genetic disorder of adrenal steroid synthesis can present with isolated premature pubic hair due to excess androgen production.
Androgen-secreting adrenal tumor
A rare but serious cause of rapid-onset hyperandrogenism that must be considered in a young child presenting with new pubic hair.
Exogenous androgen exposure
Accidental contact with androgen-containing topical medications used by an adult in the household can cause premature pubarche.
Androgen-secreting ovarian tumor
This is a very rare cause of virilization in this age group but remains a possibility for neoplastic androgen production.
eliminated: Central precocious puberty
This is ruled out by the absence of other signs of pubertal development, specifically the lack of breast development (thelarche) which typically precedes or accompanies pubarche in this condition.

differential: Juvenile granulosa cell tumor
This is the most common estrogen-secreting ovarian malignancy in prepubertal girls, perfectly matching the presentation of an ovarian mass and precocious puberty.
Functional ovarian cyst
A large, autonomous follicular cyst can produce significant estrogen, explaining the hormonal changes and the presence of a mass-like structure on ultrasound.
Ovarian thecoma
This benign stromal tumor is a well-established cause of estrogen production, leading to precocious puberty in the setting of an ovarian mass.
McCune-Albright syndrome
This syndrome causes gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty via autonomous ovarian function, which can manifest as large estrogen-producing cysts that appear as a mass.
Ovarian gonadoblastoma
This tumor can be hormonally active, secreting estrogen and causing precocious puberty, and should be considered in a child with a hormonally active ovarian mass.
eliminated: Central precocious puberty
The presence of a unilateral ovarian mass points to a peripheral, gonadotropin-independent cause rather than premature activation of the central HPG axis.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
This condition causes androgen excess and would not explain the elevated estrogen or the ovarian mass.
Premature adrenarche
This is a diagnosis of exclusion that is ruled out by the finding of a clear pathological cause for the symptoms.

differential: Granulosa cell tumor
This diagnosis is confirmed by the presence of an estrogen-producing ovarian mass with characteristic Call-Exner bodies on histopathology.
Ovarian follicular cyst
A large, functional ovarian cyst can autonomously secrete estrogen, causing peripheral precocious puberty and appearing as a mass on ultrasound.
Ovarian thecoma
This is another sex cord-stromal tumor that can be estrogen-producing, leading to a similar presentation of isosexual precocious puberty and an ovarian mass.
McCune-Albright syndrome
This genetic disorder can cause gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty via autonomously functioning ovarian cysts, which would be seen as a mass.
Ovarian gonadoblastoma
This is a rare ovarian neoplasm, typically seen in dysgenetic gonads, that can be hormonally active and present as a mass in childhood.
eliminated: Central precocious puberty
The presence of an autonomous, hormone-secreting ovarian mass indicates a peripheral (gonadotropin-independent) cause.
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
This condition causes androgen excess and would not explain the elevated estrogen or the ovarian mass.
Exogenous estrogen exposure
This would not cause the formation of an intrinsic ovarian mass seen on ultrasound.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The patient's physical examination reveals no signs of pubertal development, making granulosa cell tumor less likely as it typically presents with precocious puberty.
